claim: Many everyday life decisions require allocating finite resources, such as attention or time, to examine multiple available options.
source: Many everyday life decisions require allocating finite resources, such as attention or time, to examine multiple available options, like choosing a food supplier online.
evidence: This is a general statement about decision-making that draws from established understanding of cognitive processes.

claim: Resources can be spread across many options (breadth) or focused on a few of them (depth).
source: In cases like these, resources can be spread across many options (breadth) or focused on a few of them (depth).
evidence: This is a definitional statement establishing the breadth-depth framework.

claim: Theoretical work has described how finite resources should be allocated to maximize utility in breadth-depth problems.
source: Whilst theoretical work has described how finite resources should be allocated to maximize utility in these problems, evidence about how humans balance breadth and depth is currently lacking.
evidence: This claim references existing theoretical work without specific citations in this sentence, but is supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Evidence about how humans balance breadth and depth is currently lacking.
source: Whilst theoretical work has described how finite resources should be allocated to maximize utility in these problems, evidence about how humans balance breadth and depth is currently lacking.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: At low budget capacity, participants sample as many suppliers as possible and prefer breadth.
source: We found that at low budget capacity participants sample as many suppliers as possible, and thus prefer breadth, whereas at high capacities participants sample just a few chosen alternatives in depth, and intentionally ignore the rest.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At high capacities, participants sample just a few chosen alternatives in depth and intentionally ignore the rest.
source: We found that at low budget capacity participants sample as many suppliers as possible, and thus prefer breadth, whereas at high capacities participants sample just a few chosen alternatives in depth, and intentionally ignore the rest.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The number of alternatives sampled increases with capacity following a power law with an exponent close to 3/4.
source: The number of alternatives sampled increases with capacity following a power law with an exponent close to 3/4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: In richer environments, where good outcomes are more likely, humans further favour depth.
source: In richer environments, where good outcomes are more likely, humans further favour depth.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental manipulation of environment richness.

claim: Participants deviate from optimality and tend to allocate capacity amongst the selected alternatives more homogeneously than it would be optimal.
source: Participants deviate from optimality and tend to allocate capacity amongst the selected alternatives more homogeneously than it would be optimal, but the impact on the outcome is small.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing participant behavior to optimal model predictions.

claim: The impact of homogeneous allocation on the outcome is small.
source: Participants deviate from optimality and tend to allocate capacity amongst the selected alternatives more homogeneously than it would be optimal, but the impact on the outcome is small.
evidence: This is a finding from analyzing the consequences of the deviation from optimality.

claim: Striking the right balance between breadth and depth is critical in selecting which courses to register in college.
source: Striking the right balance between breadth and depth is critical in countless other endeavours such as when selecting which courses to register in college (Schwartz et al., 2009) or developing marketing strategies (Turner et al., 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Striking the right balance between breadth and depth is critical in developing marketing strategies.
source: Striking the right balance between breadth and depth is critical in countless other endeavours such as when selecting which courses to register in college (Schwartz et al., 2009) or developing marketing strategies (Turner et al., 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Breadth and depth search has been related to navigation through lists of search results.
source: Its implications are far reaching when it comes to understand behaviours on the internet, where breadth and depth search has been related to navigation through lists of search results (Klöckner et al., 2004) or web site menus (Miller, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Breadth and depth search has been related to navigation through web site menus.
source: Its implications are far reaching when it comes to understand behaviours on the internet, where breadth and depth search has been related to navigation through lists of search results (Klöckner et al., 2004) or web site menus (Miller, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The breadth-depth dilemma has mostly been investigated outside cognitive neuroscience.
source: Despite its relevance to understand how humans make decisions under finite resources, it is remarkable that the breadth-depth (BD) dilemma has mostly been investigated outside cognitive neuroscience (Moreno-Bote et al., 2020), in contrast to other well-studied trade-offs like speed-accuracy and exploration-exploitation (Cohen et al., 2007; Costa et al., 2019; Daw et al., 2006; Ebitz et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the literature supported by citations.

claim: Speed-accuracy and exploration-exploitation are well-studied trade-offs in cognitive neuroscience.
source: Despite its relevance to understand how humans make decisions under finite resources, it is remarkable that the breadth-depth (BD) dilemma has mostly been investigated outside cognitive neuroscience (Moreno-Bote et al., 2020), in contrast to other well-studied trade-offs like speed-accuracy and exploration-exploitation (Cohen et al., 2007; Costa et al., 2019; Daw et al., 2006; Ebitz et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The BD dilemma underlies virtually all cognitive problems.
source: The BD dilemma underlies virtually all cognitive problems, from allocating attention amongst multiple alternatives in multi-choice decision making (Busemeyer et al., 2019; Hick, 1958; Proctor and Schneider, 2018), splitting encoding precision to items in working memory (Joseph et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2014), to dividing cognitive effort into several ongoing subtasks (Feng et al., 2014; Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a broad claim about the relevance of the BD dilemma supported by citations to various cognitive domains.

claim: The BD dilemma is relevant to allocating attention amongst multiple alternatives in multi-choice decision making.
source: The BD dilemma underlies virtually all cognitive problems, from allocating attention amongst multiple alternatives in multi-choice decision making (Busemeyer et al., 2019; Hick, 1958; Proctor and Schneider, 2018), splitting encoding precision to items in working memory (Joseph et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2014), to dividing cognitive effort into several ongoing subtasks (Feng et al., 2014; Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The BD dilemma is relevant to splitting encoding precision to items in working memory.
source: The BD dilemma underlies virtually all cognitive problems, from allocating attention amongst multiple alternatives in multi-choice decision making (Busemeyer et al., 2019; Hick, 1958; Proctor and Schneider, 2018), splitting encoding precision to items in working memory (Joseph et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2014), to dividing cognitive effort into several ongoing subtasks (Feng et al., 2014; Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The BD dilemma is relevant to dividing cognitive effort into several ongoing subtasks.
source: The BD dilemma underlies virtually all cognitive problems, from allocating attention amongst multiple alternatives in multi-choice decision making (Busemeyer et al., 2019; Hick, 1958; Proctor and Schneider, 2018), splitting encoding precision to items in working memory (Joseph et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2014), to dividing cognitive effort into several ongoing subtasks (Feng et al., 2014; Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Resource allocation in decision making has been studied in simplified cases with few alternatives.
source: The dynamics of resource allocation can be very complex, and thus it has been studied in decision making in simplified cases with few alternatives (Callaway et al., 2021b; Jang et al., 2021; Krajbich et al., 2010) or in multi-tasking using a low number of simultaneously active tasks (Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Sigman and Dehaene, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Resource allocation has been studied in multi-tasking using a low number of simultaneously active tasks.
source: The dynamics of resource allocation can be very complex, and thus it has been studied in decision making in simplified cases with few alternatives (Callaway et al., 2021b; Jang et al., 2021; Krajbich et al., 2010) or in multi-tasking using a low number of simultaneously active tasks (Musslick and Cohen, 2021; Sigman and Dehaene, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In some real-life situations, feedback about the quality of resource allocation is necessarily delayed.
source: In some real-life situations, however, feedback about the quality of the allocation is necessarily delayed.
evidence: This is a general statement about real-world decision-making scenarios.

claim: Feedback can come after seconds, days, or even years in problems such as investing, choosing college, or ant colony scout exploration.
source: This happens for instance in problems such as investing (Blanchet-Scalliet et al., 2008; Reilly et al., 2016), choosing college (Schwartz et al., 2009) or, in ant colonies, sending scouts for exploration (Pratt et al., 2002); feedback can come after seconds, days, or even years.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to examples from different domains.

claim: Previous theoretical work has shown how to optimally trade off breadth and depth over multi-alternative problems where resources are allocated all at once before feedback is received.
source: Previous theoretical work has shown how to optimally trade off breadth and depth over multi-alternative problems in the situations described above, where resources are allocated all at once before feedback is received (Mastrogiuseppe and Moreno-Bote, 2022; Moreno-Bote et al., 2020; Ramírez-Ruiz and Moreno-Bote, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: At low capacity, resources should be split in as many alternatives as capacity permits (breadth) according to optimal theory.
source: A central result is that the optimal trade-off depends on the search capacity of the agent: while at low capacity resources should be split in as many alternatives as capacity permits (breadth), at high capacity resources should be focused on a relatively small number of selected alternatives so that available resources are more focused (depth) (Moreno-Bote et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from cited prior work.

claim: At high capacity, resources should be focused on a relatively small number of selected alternatives (depth) according to optimal theory.
source: A central result is that the optimal trade-off depends on the search capacity of the agent: while at low capacity resources should be split in as many alternatives as capacity permits (breadth), at high capacity resources should be focused on a relatively small number of selected alternatives so that available resources are more focused (depth) (Moreno-Bote et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from cited prior work.

claim: In rich environments, depth should be further favoured according to optimal theory.
source: In rich environments, where finding options rendering good outcomes is more likely, depth should be further favoured.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that follows from the cited work.

claim: How humans solve BD trade-offs in many-alternative decision making is largely unknown.
source: Despite of the existence of precise predictions describing ideal behaviours in these scenarios, how humans solve BD trade-offs in many-alternative decision making is largely unknown (Brown et al., 2008; Callaway et al., 2021a; Chau et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2017; Hawkins et al., 2012; Moreno-Bote et al., 2020; Roe et al., 2001; Usher and McClelland, 2004; Vul et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the literature supported by citations.

claim: Participants are presented with several virtual apricot suppliers (10 or 32) having different, and unknown, probabilities of good-quality apricots.
source: Participants played a gamified version of the task in which they were presented with several virtual apricot suppliers (10 or 32) having different, and unknown, probabilities of good-quality apricots (Materials and methods; see Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The probabilities of good-quality apricots were independently generated for each supplier in each trial from a beta prior distribution.
source: These probabilities were independently generated for each supplier in each trial from a beta prior distribution.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: At the beginning of each trial, participants received a budget of a few coins, which defined their sampling capacity in that trial.
source: At the beginning of each trial, participants received a budget of a few coins, which defined their sampling capacity in that trial.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each coin was used to buy one apricot from a selected supplier.
source: Each coin was used to buy one apricot from a selected supplier (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references a figure.

claim: Once all coins had been spent, participants discovered which of the sampled apricots were of good quality, and which ones were bad.
source: Once all coins had been spent (Figure 1b), participants discovered which of the sampled apricots were of good quality, and which ones were bad (Figure 1c), whose outcomes followed a Bernoulli process with the unknown probabilities of good-quality apricots for each supplier.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references figures.

claim: The outcomes followed a Bernoulli process with the unknown probabilities of good-quality apricots for each supplier.
source: Once all coins had been spent (Figure 1b), participants discovered which of the sampled apricots were of good quality, and which ones were bad (Figure 1c), whose outcomes followed a Bernoulli process with the unknown probabilities of good-quality apricots for each supplier.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Based on the observed outcomes, participants could estimate the probabilities from the sampled suppliers, and make a final purchase of 100 apricots from the one they considered to be the best.
source: Based on the observed outcomes, participants could estimate the probabilities from the sampled suppliers, and make a final purchase of 100 apricots from the one they considered to be the best (Figure 1d).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and references a figure.

claim: Only one of the sampled alternatives could be selected for the final purchase.
source: Only one of the sampled alternatives could be selected for the final purchase.
evidence: This describes the experimental design constraint.

claim: Participants' goal was to maximize the number of good-quality apricots collected throughout the experiment through the implementation of an informative sampling strategy.
source: Their goal was to maximize the number of good-quality apricots collected throughout the experiment through the implementation of an informative sampling strategy, adapted both to the sampling capacity and to the environment richness.
evidence: This describes the experimental task goal.

claim: The task was intuitive and easily grasped by most participants.
source: The task was intuitive and easily grasped by most participants.
evidence: This is an observation about participant understanding of the task.

claim: No instructions about the underlying probability generative model was provided as the context was informative enough to aid task understanding.
source: No instructions about the underlying probability generative model was provided as the context was informative enough to aid task understanding (Schustek et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental design decision, supported by a citation.

claim: Two different ranges of sampling capacity, narrow (2–10 samples per trial) and wide (2–32), were tested.
source: Two different ranges of sampling capacity, narrow (2–10 samples per trial) and wide (2–32), were tested to zoom-in relevant behavioural regimes (see Materials and methods and Table 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Three environments were used differing in the parameters of the beta distribution: poor (mean 0.25), neutral (mean 0.50), and rich (mean 0.75).
source: For each range, we used three environments differing in the parameters of the beta distribution used to generate probabilities of good-quality apricots for each supplier. By increasing the average probability of good alternatives, we can increase the richness of the environment to move from a 'poor', to a 'neutral', up to a 'rich' environment (beta prior means: poor, 0.25; neutral, 0.50; and rich, 0.75).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Environments and capacity ranges were run in a block fashion, with capacity in each chosen randomly in each trial from the underlying range in that block.
source: While environments and capacity ranges were run in a block fashion, capacity in each was chosen randomly in each trial from the underlying range in that block.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Environments were tested within and between subjects in two different sets of experiments, to address potential learning effects.
source: Environments were tested within and between subjects in two different sets of experiments, to address potential learning effects.
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: At higher capacities, sampling progressively evolves towards a trade-off between breadth and depth.
source: At higher capacities, sampling progressively evolves towards a trade-off between breadth and depth.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: A fast transition between the low- and high-capacity regimes was not observed, contrary to predictions.
source: Although these are predicted features and thus signs of optimal behaviour, we did not observe a fast transition between the low- and high-capacity regimes, as previously predicted (Moreno-Bote et al., 2020, see also Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding comparing the data to theoretical predictions.

claim: The smoothness of transitions could result from averaging over participants having different transition points, or by having allocation noise.
source: This could simply result from averaging over participants having different transition points, or by having allocation noise, which would smooth out fast transitions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed deviation from predictions.

claim: Models with allocation noise account for the smoothness of transitions and are better models in predicting the behaviour than the noise-free optimal model.
source: As shown below, models with allocation noise account for the smoothness of this transitions and are better models in predicting the behaviour than the noise-free optimal model.
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Richer environments typically cause a stronger preference for depth sampling.
source: The effect of environmental richness was also clearly visible in our data, with richer environments typically causing a stronger preference for depth sampling (Figure 2A–B; different colours), consistent with predictions.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Participants' strategy was overall strongly dependent on environment richness, as predicted.
source: Therefore, as it becomes easier for the participant to find good options, they prefer to neglect an even larger number of suppliers and focus capacity to examine fewer ones. We also observed systematic deviations from optimality (Figure 2A; black lines). In particular, despite participants' strategy was overall strongly dependent on environment richness, as predicted, this was mostly due to a strong effect of the poor environment (Figure 2A–B; red lines), whereas they were not sensitive to the difference between neutral and rich environments (green and blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The dependence on environment richness was mostly due to a strong effect of the poor environment.
source: In particular, despite participants' strategy was overall strongly dependent on environment richness, as predicted, this was mostly due to a strong effect of the poor environment (Figure 2A–B; red lines), whereas they were not sensitive to the difference between neutral and rich environments (green and blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Participants were not sensitive to the difference between neutral and rich environments.
source: In particular, despite participants' strategy was overall strongly dependent on environment richness, as predicted, this was mostly due to a strong effect of the poor environment (Figure 2A–B; red lines), whereas they were not sensitive to the difference between neutral and rich environments (green and blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A decrease of the exponent as the environment gets richer was observed in three designs.
source: Overall, we observed in the three designs mentioned a decrease of the exponent as the environment gets richer.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The decrease in exponent suggests an adaptation of participants' sampling behaviour to the environment, with sampling depth increasing with the richness of environment.
source: This suggests an adaptation of participants' sampling behaviour to the environment, with sampling depth increasing with the richness of environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings.

claim: At high capacity, the difference between optimal and observed M tends to be negative, especially noticeable in the neutral and rich environments.
source: In contrast, at high capacity this difference tends to be negative, which is especially noticeable in the neutral and rich environments.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Participants have a bias to sample more deeply than optimal at low capacities while this bias is reversed at high capacities.
source: The results of these analyses indicate some deviations from optimality. Participants have a bias to sample more deeply than optimal at low capacities while this bias is reversed at high capacities.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data findings.

claim: Overall biases could be accounted for by assuming that participants have a biased model of the richness of the environment.
source: These overall biases could be accounted for by assuming that participants have a biased model of the richness of the environment, not estimating as much as they should the extreme nature of poor or rich environments (Schustek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed biases, supported by a citation.

claim: Through experience within a block, participants become closer to optimal.
source: Therefore, through experience within a block, participants become closer to optimal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings about learning within blocks.

claim: Participants' sampling strategy in the neutral environment seems to differ depending on whether it was presented first or not.
source: For instance, participants' sampling strategy in the neutral environment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 middle panels) seems to differ depending on whether it was presented first or not.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: If the neutral environment was presented after the poor environment, a clear deviation towards breadth was observed.
source: If presented after the poor environment, we observe a clear deviation towards breadth, whereas a shift towards depth is observed if presented after the rich environment.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: If the neutral environment was presented after the rich environment, a shift towards depth was observed.
source: If presented after the poor environment, we observe a clear deviation towards breadth, whereas a shift towards depth is observed if presented after the rich environment.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Participants' sampling strategy was affected by the previous environment presented and adaptation to a new environment requires overcoming the behavioural pattern implemented at earlier blocks.
source: Although based on exploratory analyses, these observations provide some evidence that participants' sampling strategy was affected by the previous environment presented and that adaptation to a new environment requires to overcome the behavioural pattern implemented at earlier blocks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the exploratory data findings.

claim: The carryover effects from the previously used strategy are long-lived.
source: Therefore, the carryover effects from the previously used strategy are long-lived.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings about persistence of carryover effects.

claim: Using binomial noise, the free power-law model outperforms all five other models.
source: Using binomial noise, the free power-law model outperforms all five other models (Figure 8A and Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The optimal model is better at predicting participants' sampling strategy than the pure breadth, depth, and square root models.
source: The optimal model, even though less efficient than the power model, is better at predicting participants' sampling strategy than the pure breadth, depth, and square root models.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The outcomes of model comparison are mostly equivalent when using the Gaussian noise model.
source: The outcomes of model comparison are mostly equivalent when using the Gaussian noise model (for the results of this model, see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 5), and therefore we restrict our discussion to the binomial noise model from now on.
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis.

claim: The free power-law model outperforms any other models in all environments.
source: Additionally, the free power-law model once again outperforms any other models in all environments (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from model comparison analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Participants frequently allocated the samples homogeneously across the selected alternatives.
source: We observed that participants frequently allocated the samples homogeneously across the selected alternatives, a sampling strategy which in most cases differs largely from optimal allocation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There was an overall bias towards homogenous sampling, and this bias was stronger as the environment was richer.
source: That is, there was an overall bias towards homogenous sampling, and this bias was stronger as the environment was richer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings.

claim: Participants select the optimal sampled alternative according to the normative rule on 96.0 ± 4.34% of the trials.
source: We observed that participants select the optimal sampled alternative according to the above rule on 96.0 ± 4.34% (mean ± s.d.) of the trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The BD dilemma is related to exploration-exploitation but has the crucial difference that a limited resource can be divided into several options simultaneously.
source: The BD dilemma, studied here, is related to EE but has the crucial difference that a limited resource can be divided into several options simultaneously.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction drawn by the authors.

claim: Both exploration and exploitation could a priori be performed in parallel and interact with each other in the BD dilemma.
source: Therefore, both exploration and exploitation could a priori be performed in parallel and interact with each other.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the BD dilemma.

claim: The divisibility of the agent's resource results in a qualitatively new problem compared to exploration-exploitation.
source: These trade-offs do not naturally arise in the EE, as it is the divisibility of the agent's resource, and thus a new degree of freedom, what results in a qualitatively new problem.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction drawn by the authors.

claim: Participants' strategy is overall strongly dependent on environment richness, as predicted.
source: Consistent with theoretical predictions, we observe that, at low capacity, a pure-breadth strategy is favoured (sampling as many alternatives as possible), while as capacity increases, participants progressively sample relatively fewer of them in more depth. Additionally, our results reveal that participants' sampling strategy adapts to the environment with richer environments promoting depth over breadth.
evidence: This is a summary of findings consistent with theoretical predictions.

claim: Human behaviour is close to, but systematically deviated, from optimality.
source: We observe that human behaviour is close to, but systematically deviated, from optimality.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Participants' sampling strategy does not follow the predicted optimal model but is better captured by a power law.
source: Regarding the number of alternatives sampled as a function of capacity, we observe that participants' sampling strategy does not follow the predicted optimal model but is better captured by a power law.
evidence: This is a summary of the model comparison findings.

claim: The power law strategy has the advantage to be continuous (no break point), which might contribute to reduce computational cost.
source: This strategy has the advantage to be continuous (no break point), which might contribute to reduce computational (hence, cognitive) cost, within a controlled loss of efficiency.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed strategy.

claim: Deviations from optimality may be explained by errors in the estimation of the environment richness.
source: Given that environment richness is not known precisely by participants, such results may be explained by errors in the estimation of the environment richness (Drugowitsch et al., 2016; Schustek et al., 2019; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The bias towards an even distribution of samples may emerge to simplify computations during sampling.
source: At a cognitive level, such bias towards an even distribution of samples may have various origins. It could emerge to simplify computations during sampling due to an even division of samples, which might be easier to remember and implement as a motor output.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed bias.

claim: Homogeneous allocation can emerge to simplify comparisons during choice by making it easier to compare fractions with a common denominator.
source: It can also emerge to simplify comparisons during choice in at least two ways. First, it is easier to compare fractions with a common denominator, thus reducing cognitive load.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed bias.

claim: A homogeneous allocation of samples ensures that alternatives are equally risky, as they carry the same amount of information.
source: Second, a homogeneous allocation of samples ensures that alternatives are equally risky, as they carry the same amount of information.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed bias.

claim: Humans have shown a preference to sample the most uncertain option.
source: Indeed, humans have shown a preference to sample (note, not choose) the most uncertain option (Alméras et al., 2021; Lewis, 1995; Schulz et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2021), a heuristic strategy that has been called 'uncertainty directed exploration'.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Homogenous sampling could have other sources, such as the human preference for symmetry.
source: Homogenous sampling could also have other sources, such as the human preference for symmetry (Attneave, 1955).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Participants focus more on the number of samples per alternative over the number of sampled alternatives.
source: Our results suggest that participants focus more on the number of samples per alternative over the number of sampled alternatives (see Figure 10).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Participants' bias to sample homogenously may drive, at least in part, deviations from optimality observed in the number of sampled alternatives.
source: Consequently, participants' bias to sample homogenously may drive, at least in part, deviations from optimality observed in the number of sampled alternatives.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting different findings.

claim: Deviations towards either breadth or depth may partially originate from a participants' will to reduce uncertainty about either finding a 'good' alternative or correctly estimating the reward.
source: We hypothesize that deviations towards either breadth or depth may partially originate from a participants' will to reduce uncertainty about either finding a 'good' alternative during the sampling phase (one with positive outcome(s)) or correctly estimating the reward during the purchase phase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Deep sampling enables to better estimate the success probability of the sampled alternatives but at the risk of not having any good one.
source: On the one hand, deep sampling enables to better estimate the success probability of the sampled alternatives in order to find the best one but at the risk of not having any good one.
evidence: This is a conceptual explanation of the trade-off.

claim: Deep sampling strategy is more reward centred and may be followed by individuals with low risk aversion.
source: This strategy is more reward centred and may be followed by individuals with low risk aversion.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about individual differences.

claim: Sampling broadly reduces the risk not to find any good alternative and might be followed by individuals with higher risk aversion profiles.
source: On the other hand, sampling broadly reduces the risk not to find any good alternative. Such a strategy might be more cautious and may be followed by individuals with higher risk aversion profiles.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about individual differences.

claim: Mathematical knowledge may have influenced the way participants comprehend and behave in the task.
source: Finally, even though our paradigm was introduced using a real-life narrative to facilitate understanding and avoid using a mathematical or probabilistic-related vocabulary, we cannot exclude that mathematical knowledge has influenced the way participants comprehend and behave in the task.
evidence: This is a speculative consideration about potential confounds.

claim: The heuristics identified (continuous power-law sampling strategy and homogenous sampling) are associated with a lower cognitive effort compared to the optimal behaviour.
source: In general, even though participants engage in behaviours which deviate significantly from optimality, the heuristics identified – continuous power-law sampling strategy and homogenous sampling – are associated with a lower cognitive effort compared to the optimal behaviour.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: If following these biases impacts significantly the outcome, the loss remains relatively small in the task.
source: Additionally, if following these biases impact significantly the outcome, the loss remains relatively small in our task.
evidence: This is a finding from the outcome analysis.

claim: It is not clear whether these biases reflect participants' computational limitations (bounded rationality) or are the result of a compromise between the error in the sampling strategy and the cost associated with brain computations (bounded optimality or resource rationality).
source: It is not clear whether these biases reflect participants' computational limitations – bounded rationality (Simon, 1955) – or are the result of a compromise between the error in the sampling strategy and the cost associated with brain computations – bounded optimality (Russell and Subramanian, 2009) or resource rationality (Griffiths et al., 2015; Lieder et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a discussion of alternative theoretical interpretations with citations.

claim: None of the reported deviations can easily be explained by the presence of motor biases.
source: Importantly, none of the reported deviations can easily be explained by the presence of motor biases, as samples are allocated one by one and participants always must go to the screen centre to drag the next sample to a supplier, so that the distance to any supplier is identical and any motion direction asymmetry is the same sample to sample.
evidence: This is an argument ruling out a potential confound based on the experimental design.

claim: The study cannot be explained by choice overload.
source: Further, despite the large number of alternatives presented in the apricot task (either 10 or 32), we did not find evidence that participants considered much fewer options than the optimal number, and therefore our study cannot be explained by – and offers a counter-example of – choice overload (Iyengar and Lepper, 2000; Kuksov and Villas-Boas, 2010; Sethi-Iyengar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature with citations.

claim: At larger capacities, participants tend to consider more alternatives than optimal.
source: On the contrary, at larger capacities, participants tend to consider more alternatives than optimal.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing participant data to optimal predictions.

claim: No information about any alternative was directly accessible to the participant before the outcome of the allocation was revealed.
source: In our experimental setup, no information about any alternative was directly accessible to the participant before the outcome of the allocation was revealed, which may prevent perturbations and biases in the decision process by facilitating the a priori consideration of all alternatives on an equal footing.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and its potential impact.

claim: Contamination happens in participants' sampling strategy when presented with different environments consecutively.
source: Concerning the effect of environment richness, we suspect contamination to happen in participants' sampling strategy when presented with different environments consecutively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about sequential effects.

claim: The use of between-subjects designs should be favoured to thwart contamination effects.
source: The use of between-subjects designs should be favoured to thwart this effect.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the findings.

claim: The framework has the advantage to be easily adapted to investigate future questions.
source: Taking into consideration these observations, our framework has the advantage to be easily adapted to investigate future questions.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential of the experimental paradigm.

claim: This is the first thorough experimental study of the BD dilemma.
source: To conclude, we have developed the first thorough experimental study of the BD dilemma, which, benefiting from a large adaptability and capability to translate real-life situations, offers a promising framework to study many-alternative human decision making under finite resources.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The results reveal the use of close-to-optimal choice behaviours which are both sensitive to the capacity and the environment.
source: Already, our results reveal the use of close-to-optimal choice behaviours which are both sensitive to the capacity and the environment and identify some of the heuristics used to simplify computations at the cost of optimality.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.
